utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While Mr. Ciaglinski is coming in, one administrative matter I might deal with. It relates to an event during the evidence of the witness Sabri Popaj. There was objection taken to a video and, the Court suggested that the matter of identifying the Belaj bridge could be achieved by a still being produced from the video. The Prosecution have now uploaded such a still numbered P2474. The Chamber is minded to admit that but not to admit the video unless there is any objection to that course of action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see none, so we shall admit that, Mr. Hannis, and not admit the video itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ciaglinski.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to continue with the cross-examination by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, I hope to be rather brief. I have only 7 to 10 minutes worth of questions for you, so bear with me. Now, Colonel, during your direct examination you testified about your return to Pristina after the conclusion of the NATO campaign and the burning documents you saw and photographed. Now, first of all, the one picture that you showed us of the truck with the smoldering smoke behind it, first of all, how many days after your return to Pristina was this picture taken, if you can recall.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was taken on the second or third day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And am I correct that this -- this location behind the truck is where you previously had described a large -- I think you had described it as a truckload worth of documents burning for several days. Is that the same -- the same location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, am I correct that the location you photographed is actually the passageway between two out of the multiple -- I think it's five buildings of the MUP complex in the centre of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the complex which faces the main road. Yes, you're quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And is this the complex that during your time as part of the KVM mission you knew to have housed many offices, including the Pristina SUP headed Colonel Petric whom you mention in your statement, and a separate building that housed the MUP staff, separate building for the gaol, separate building for state security, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they were government offices. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Great. And is this also the same complex where you saw the major antenna at the rear that you described in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, the buildings fronting the road then had another building behind, and between that building and the stadium complex where was are antenna was. So, if you like, it's the whole collection of buildings but it is not the building I was referring to. The building I referred to Colonel Mijatovic had his office or the building -- was this building but the building behind, if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Still part of the same overall complex though?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I think -- I think we'd agreed yesterday that the antenna at the time you returned back had been destroyed; you don't know when. Now, are you aware that one of the buildings in the complex housed archives and storage of documents including old documents that had expired? Did anyone make you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because we had no access to these buildings during our time with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And are you aware or did you find out whether in fact any or in fact all of the buildings in this complex had been evacuated and left into disuse sometime before the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building that we occupied where we had our offices and overlooked the pile of burning paper was still in the process of being evacuated. So it was not actually empty of personnel or documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware that under the Kumanovo accords the Serb authorities were required to empty the buildings in this complex and to take out all old documents to accommodate the arrival of KFOR?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, but I'll bow to you again on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you or your interpreter take note of any of the expiration dates or validity dates of any of the documents you saw burning?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We looked at the general sort of context of what the documents were. I mean dates were -- we looked at dates, but I can't remember off the top of my head whether they were a year old or five years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the documents included in addition to passports and IDs also applications for passports and IDs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe you indicated that you had retained certain exemplars or samples of items from the fire. First of all, what types of documents did you retain these samples of, what were they? Were they IDs, were they applications for IDs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All of those. And where are these documents now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I passed the documents on to General DZ, who passed them to the OSCE authorities in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did do you recall when it was that you passed these documents to General Drewienkiewicz?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure whether I gave them to him immediately or when we returned to Skopje a couple of weeks later, but they were certainly handed back to him. And I discussed it with him some time ago, during the Milosevic trial -- following the Milosevic trial, and he confirms that this was -- this was the case. He remembers taking the documents off me and passing them to the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what quantity of documents we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a handful.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A wedge of documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, I'd like to turn just for a moment for a couple of questions relating to Mr. Lukic and the MUP staff based upon your knowledge and interaction with them. First of all, you mentioned Colonel Mijatovic during your testimony. Did you know or was it explained to you that Colonel Mijatovic was in fact appointed to liaise with the KVM by Minister of the Interior Stojiljkovic and that in fact in this position he represented the entire MUP of the Republic of Serbia, quite separate from his duties and functions at the MUP staff with General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. He never sort of made -- made us aware of this. We always assumed he was working directly to General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he would always defer back to General Lukic, never to any authorities in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I believe you mentioned in your statements and perhaps in your testimony that General Lukic met with someone named Hilsep. Am I correct that from January 1999 onwards a general -- General Hilsep had been appointed by General DZ to liaise with the MUP. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was General Richard Hislop, an Irish officer, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know how often General Hislep met with General Lukic and the duration and nature of their meetings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am away of that towards the end of our mission in the last few weeks it was fairly frequently but before that not so frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And during --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you spell Hislop for us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's spelled Haeslip but pronounced Hislop, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, spell it out, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's like H-a-e-s-l-i-p, Haeslip, but pronounced Hislop. I'm not very good at Irish -- certain Irish names.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Trying to see if I can be of assistance in the documents but I'm not finding it right now.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a brigadier general.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right. In any event, moving on, is -- as part of these frequent meetings towards the end of the KVM stay in Kosovo and Metohija, you don't have any -- you don't have knowledge of any of the matters that were discussed or the many requests by General Haeslip that General Lukic acceded to, do you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in very general terms, that it was to do with -- certainly with our evacuation. It was to do with the general state of affairs at the time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And lastly in your statement you described Sreten Lukic that you knew at that time to be a lieutenant general. Are you in fact aware that at the time of the KVM mission Sreten Lukic was actually a major general? And upon what was your knowledge of his rank based?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I -- maybe I was just being very generous in promoting General Lukic. I don't know. It was just a slip, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think I have any more questions for this witness. Thank you very much for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Colonel Ciaglinski, good afternoon. My name is Norman Sepenuk. I'm an attorney for General Ojdanic, and I have a very brief series of questions for you. You testified in direct examination that Colonel Kotur told you about an alleged plan to expel the KLA and the Albanian civilian population from Kosovo. Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you further testified in the Milosevic trial that you told General DZ about this; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you -- you testified specifically in the Milosevic trial, and it's at page 3333, you said, "I was given this information. I then passed it on to DZ who chose not to believe it." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then you further testified at the Milosevic trial in answer to a question by Judge Kwon, and this is at pages 3354 and 5 of the record, and I quote, you said: "Well, you know," this is General DZ saying this to you, sir. You said: "General DZ said, 'Well, you know, this is just possibly one man's opinion.'" And you said you tried to argue him -- argue with him about that because it was so detailed but he just put it to one side. Is that a pretty fair summary of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in the Milosevic trial General DZ was asked about this, on page 3070, and he said, in effect: "There was no plan to expel that I know of." And he said precisely, and I quote: "I saw no plan. Nobody talked to me about a plan." You -- and I take it you followed the Milosevic trial and have I quoted that correctly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you make a written report to General DZ about this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't because of the time constraints on what we were actually doing at the time and we were already destroying documents, destroying computer hard drives. There was very little to make me actually write it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you didn't make -- the short of it is you didn't make a written report to General DZ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Nor did you -- nor, as I understand it, did you make a written report to anyone in OSCE about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Turning to one last area, and I'll ask you, sir, would you agree that under the October 1998 verification agreements, the three agreements that you said you carried around in your pockets, that your mandate was to be a neutral and detached -- detached observer of events?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in other words, you shouldn't favour one side over the other. You shouldn't favour the Serbs over the KLA; you shouldn't favour the KLA over the Serbs. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. Sorry, I'm just pausing to give the interpreters time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. And you were working primarily with Serb forces, and is it fair to say you wanted the Serbs to trust you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And it's fair to say the Serbs didn't trust the KLA, so at the very least you wanted them to trust you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, a working relationship is based on trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. And you testified as an example of that trust that on -- that on at least one occasion you were given maps by the Serbian army to use which you did not pass on to anyone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pass them on to the KLA. They came within the OSCE so they were not passed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And in fact you also testified yesterday that you didn't aid the KLA in any of their activities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not aid the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you disclose information received from Serb forces to NATO?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You did not. Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends when.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, as I understand it that you were -- tell me about this. You went to Macedonia after Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in Macedonia what was your position there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had several positions in Macedonia. I was the liaison -- the OSCE liaison to NATO. I was also working alongside UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And while you were in Macedonia did you at any time, or indeed at any time during your OSCE employment, that's from late December 1998 through until, what, June 13th of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you at any time during that period provide or assist in providing information to NATO about the deployment and location of Serbian forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. As -- as a NATO officer myself and as our mission had finished in Kosovo, then I presumed I was free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And how about the maps, for example, that you received from the Serbian forces? Did you provide them to -- to NATO forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't, but I believe the maps were used by NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in the -- in the Milosevic trial you were asked a question by Judge May, and the question was: "Colonel," to you, "can" you assist as to this: It's alleged that the KLA and NATO were working together. As far as you are concerned, was there any evidence of that?" And your answer was: "No." Are you now changing your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've said that the KLA and NATO were working together. I can't remember when I said this in the last few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, I'm quoting from page 3263 of the Milosevic trial. And at that point Mr. Milosevic was sort of making a statement. He says: "I suppose it's clear to you, we can see from what took place. We can also see from the statements that the so-called commanders of these terrorist KLA groups that NATO Air Force were the air forces of the KLA because they actually worked in cahoots together. Is that something you're aware of or not?" And then Judge May interjected, said: "This is getting well away from the witness's evidence. It's a matter of comment by you. And if you have evidence of it, you can call it in due course." And then Judge May asked you this specific question, and I'll repeat it: "Colonel, can you assist us in this? It's alleged that the KLA and NATO were working together. As far as you were concerned, was there any evidence of that," and you said: "No." Is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, there is there a problem with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's clear now. Before I think there was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So, in other words, there's no evidence that you would know of that NATO and the KLA were working together, including the time you were in Macedonia? Okay. Now, you do you know a person named Afrim Aziri?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And tell us about him.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was General DZ's driver and then he became my driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Is he a respectable gentleman?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He used to be, I believe, an officer in the Serbian air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. So would you believe what -- what he would say if he was under oath? Would you believe him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no reason why I shouldn't but, you know, I don't know what's in someone else's mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I will tell you this, Colonel, and in America we have an expression inquiring before firing. You don't make allegations, even suggest allegations, that somebody's done something improper unless you ask him about it, and that's all I'm doing with you now, sir. I make no allegations about anything, but I do have information here that seems to contradict, seems to contradict what you said, so I simply want to ask you about it. The information could be erroneous, it could be wrong, so I'm simply going to ask you to explain it. And before I do, I want to ask you again: To your knowledge, did the KLA commanders pass information to Mr. Aziri about the deployment of Serb forces in Kosovo, the location of Serb weaponry, the quantity of weaponry, and the specific locations of Serb troops?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can tell you is that when I arrived with Afrim in Kosovo he worked for me for a very shorted time and then worked for me no longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you don't recall that then?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And then your testimony further is that you didn't discuss this with him, the deployment of Serb troops, location of weaponry, that kind of thing; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw him a few times, and he would ask me about what I knew about Serbian deployments in Kosovo and if I knew of any plans, and I believe I also had done an interview in Macedonia with ABC television which went out on ABC, and I at that time I think I spoke for 20 minutes about what I thought was called the horseshoe plan. So this wasn't something that wasn't unknown and people knew that I actually had evidence or information about such a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. Well, I'm not talking about horseshoe now; I'm talking about something more general, okay? And did you suggest to Mr. Aziri that perhaps he should share information about the deployment of Serb forces weaponry and whatnot with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You can't recall that. Okay. And I take it you can't recall passing along any information to that effect to NATO concerning Serb forces, the deployment thereof, Serb weaponry, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- nothing -- Aziri to NATO [inaudible].

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'm going to ask you to look at defendant 3D402, if that could be put on the screen. And with the indulgence of the trial panel, could you take the time to read that statement, and if I could respectfully ask Your Honours to take a look at that statement. If the ushers, as they're doing, would just slowly scroll so that the statement can be read. I think Colonel Ciaglinski is indicating that he'd like to see more of it. So if you'd just keep scrolling up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's move it quite quickly, please. I can see nothing at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And if you indicate, Colonel, when you finish reading it, and with the permission and indulgence of the Trial Chamber if we can then scroll up a little bit more, but I don't want to go too fast, give everybody a chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think everyone has had time. Let's move it up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. You've had a chance to read it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: First of all, let me ask you: Did you have a general comment about it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm surprised that -- well, in some ways I'm not surprised that Afrim would write this but -- because he was a fairly -- I mean, okay, he was a nice man and the reason we sacked him was he was quite unreliable as a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: As a driver?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. But I take it, do you change what you said before that you had no reason to disbelieve what -- anything he would say?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I read this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So, in other words, this is not true. Is the whole statement false?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Tell us what's false about it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we go back, please, to the previous page? As you know from earlier evidence given that the -- the contacts with the KLA -- I mean, I didn't have contacts with the KLA, so I had no way of receiving anything or sending anything to the KLA. The person who had contact was -- one of them was David Wilson. The other one was David Meyer, and David Meyer was the man with the sat firm and the sat faxes. And David Meyer, I believe, was the man probably dealing with Afrim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, he says -- I'll ask you then something specific. He says in his statement that: "The UCK commanders were passing information along to me about the deployment of Serb forces in Kosova, the location of Serb weaponry, the quantity of weaponry, and the specific location of Serb troops. This information was initially being gathered for the OSCE management. Richard Ciaglinski and David Meyer discussed this information with me and suggested that it should perhaps be shared with NATO command. I agreed it was a must." Is that a true estimate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's -- I've answered part of that because there's one complete paragraph, isn't it, stop --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Sure.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Information initially being gathered for the OSCE." Well, I wouldn't know, because if the UCK commanders were passing this information as -- I've already explained it was David Meyer that would have been talking to Afrim, if anyone. What else can I say about that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you actually deny speaking with him at all about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Afrim?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have heard something about it, but I had nothing to do about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You might have heard something about it? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, about the -- Afrim was always trying to sort of -- he was telling myself and others that he could actually get in touch with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: He says specifically that he discussed it with you and Mr. Meyer, and that you and Mr. Meyer suggested that the information perhaps be shared with NATO command. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Could it have been -- could it have happened and you can't -- you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You don't think so or you know so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a fairly major statement, isn't it, so -- but I'm saying no, I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And he goes on to say: "Richard Ciaglinski was already in touch with NATO, so we all agreed that he would pass this information along to NATO." Is that a true statement or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, part of it is. Richard was in touch with NATO, because that was my role. I was the OSCE link to NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you agree to pass this information along to NATO?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I passed nothing to NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And the statement further goes on to say that: "Richard has some friends who have been receiving fax messages from the UCK and handing them to me for translation." Was that -- is that true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have -- I didn't have any friends in the -- in the UCK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And he also talks about a letter that was received from -- from KLA to pass along to General Clark, the commander of NATO forces, a letter of 19 April 1999. Did you ever see such a letter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Might you have?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe if you show it to me I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, I have a problem about showing it to you, because we have not included this as a -- an exhibit for cross. I have the letter in my hand, but I don't know whether I would get permission of the Trial Chamber to exhibit it to you, and I don't know if Mr. Hannis would object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Frankly, Your Honour, we received this from the Prosecution, and -- but it's not -- you know, we can just deal with it in our part of the case, if necessary. I have a hard copy here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As long as Mr. Sepenuk will remember he owes me one I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: According to my -- according to -- I missed that, Mr. Hannis, I'm sorry. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's just pointing out that if he takes no objection you owe him one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Oh. I might owe him less than that, Your Honour, because Mr. Visnjic tells me that it's already -- it's in the system but it hasn't -- it wasn't identified in an e-mail to Mr. Hannis, which I regret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be that it doesn't help on the issue anyway because it's more to do with direct contact between the KLA with NATO in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Except that Mr. Afrim Aziri says that this letter was passed along directly to -- because he says: "It is my understanding that a copy of that translation has been given to General Clark," and I was simply wondering -- it's 4D32, as a matter of fact. The letter is 4D32. And the only thing is I did not -- I don't believe our e-mail to -- to Mr. Hannis mentioned that exhibit number. So technically we're in violation of the court rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you may refer to it. There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So why you don't you take a look. If you could put that on the screen, 4D32. Just take a look at that letter, Colonel, and tell us whether you recognise that letter.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You've never seen that letter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Of course it's Mr. Afrim Aziri's statement that that letter was turned over to General Clark. Right. So I will -- and your answer is no, you have --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you finally, having seen the contents of Mr. Afrim Aziri's statement and what he says about your role in turning over documents to the KLA, I'll ask you finally that question from Judge May when he said: Colonel, can you assist us as to this: It is alleged that the KLA and NATO were working together. As far as you were concerned, was there any evidence of that?" You said: "No." Is that, sir, your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one matter. It is not a question, it is a clarification with the witness about the certain name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, during your testimony yesterday, the reference is row -- page 68, row 20 and 21. You were referring to a person named -- named here in the transcript Guy Sans. I believe the -- would you be so kind to -- to spell his last name, please, just for the record, because it is spelled as S-a-n-s in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's -- it's certainly S-a-n-d-s, but I can't remember if it had an E, because he's American but a strange American. No aspersions are being cast anywhere. But, no, he's -- it might have been S-a-n-d-s or S-a-n-d-e-s, I'm not sure. It's not S-a-n-s for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. That's all I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zecevic. I take it the reference to strangeness was to spelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'm outnumbered, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we show the witness Exhibit 2D8.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, Mr. Petrovic asked you on Monday about the commission for cooperation, and he showed you a document which maybe you'll see on your screen in a moment which related to the make-up of the commission in Belgrade, and I think you'll recall it listed Mr. Sainovic as president but then it names, as you can see now, 11 members of the commission.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can scroll down to those. Of those 11, did you know any of these individuals or were any of them present in Pristina attending meetings of the commission that met in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if number 9, if that's the administrator in Kosovo, Zoran Andjelkovic, then, yes, I was -- I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And then we saw a supplement yesterday that there were two additional members added later and that was Colonel Loncar and I believe it was Dragoljub Janovic from the Ministry of Justice. We now Loncar was in Pristina, how about Minister of Justice, Mr. Janovic? Was he ever in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't come across him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in Pristina, the representatives that you met with in connection with the commission for cooperation, when Loncar and Andjelkovic were both present, which one was in charge of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Loncar was -- when he was there, he ran the meetings. I mean, he told us at one point that - I read my notes today - he was the representative of the FRY government in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you've said in your statement and in your testimony that there was at least one occasion when Mr. Sainovic came to town and was present at a meeting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who presided at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday at page 6880, line 10, Mr. Petrovic was asking you about whether or not it was a fact that the KLA rearmed and reinforced and consolidated militarily during OSCE's presence there in late 1998 and early 1999, and you agreed that was true. What about the VJ and the MUP during that period of time? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 6891, line 8. Judge Bonomy asked you a question to clarify something about the prisoners that you were visiting in Nis, and I think you clarified those were KLA prisoners, but you had made a reference to a number of soldiers as well, and I think you explained those were VJ soldiers and there was some kind of exchange involving those. Can you tell us briefly what that was all about and how was OSCE involved in that matter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the Serbian side wanted to get its soldiers back which had been -- who had been captured just east of Vucitrn-Mitrovica area, and obviously the KLA weren't going to release them when they knew that there were also KLA prisoners sitting somewhere in Serbia. So following several meetings but at very high level it was agreed that there would be an exchange of prisoners, but the exchange of prisoners could not be seen as an exchange of prisoners so there had to be a gap, a time gap, between the relies of one and the realise of the others of the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say this discussion took place at very high levels --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who were the representatives on the respective sides in these high-level negotiations about this exchange that was not going to be an exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the Serbian side it was usually led by Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about on the KLA side, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. If the KLA were involved in these meetings I didn't go to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from OSCE, was anyone involved in this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I believe you know -- I don't know if Mr. Walker was present but certainly that was either the ambassador or DZ or somebody from the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know -- you said there had been a gap in between. Who went first?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We released the VJ soldiers first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why -- why was it being required that this not be seen as a -- a direct exchange, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know, and it was - it was purely that -- it wasn't for showing any weakness of government caving in to the KLA, caving in to terrorists that this sort of exchange would take place and also probably not to set any precedents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday - I want to go to another Defence lawyer - Mr. Cepic asked you some questions, and at page 6895, line 12, he was talking about inspections of VJ facilities, and he asked you about the problem that the army would have with no notice on inspections and a requirement to have 24 hours notice. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the purposes of your mission, was it important to be able to do inspections on little notice or no notice?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there were reinforcements coming in all the time and equipments were coming in, and we were actually beginning to loose track of what was actually in Kosovo and what had gone out of Kosovo and therefore it was important to verify what was there, in agreement with the original agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 6895, line 22 he mentioned that one of the agreements that was worked out in connection with this locally, I guess, was that there was a requirement for the presence of a liaison officer from the VJ when you were going to do some of these inspections. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you said you helped draft that provision?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the -- I did. I mean, I actually issued the instruction and took it round the regional centres myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when that came to be a requirement, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And did that apply only in the area of the border belt or all across Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was specifically intended for the border belt because that's where the problems were. However, Colonel Kotur and General Loncar did actually want -- also required us if our verifiers wanted to visit a military installation, but not to verify but just to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At page 6896, line 14 he asked you about the VJ's training, exercise and training locations. I think in your answer you indicated that you were told the VJ's position about training was that they could train anywhere in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Initially they were saying they were deployed to certain areas and then when they deployed there they said they were deployed somewhere else, and when I questioned it they said they could deploy anywhere, because the whole of Kosovo was a training area for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did -- didn't you understand that to include Kosovo Albanian villages?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was obvious that when they deployed the areas did include Kosovo Albanian villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's already too late, Your Honour. I think we got clear answers from this witness in the examination-in-chief when Mr. Hannis questioned the witness on this same subject that he's raising again, but thank you anyway for hearing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When they -- when you saw VJ units go out in the field and deploy, did you actually see this occur where they settle up a perimeter for a training area that encompassed a Kosovo Albanian village?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you allowed in to inspect this particular deployment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, there were several but one we were not allowed in until we got clearances by satellite telephone to go in, and certainly another area towards the -- right towards the end, again sort of south of Vucitrn where there had been a lot of shelling and fighting going on, we were not allowed actually towards the villages but we could see the burning villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then later at page 6913, line 10 Mr. Cepic asked you about -- I think it's Lapastica near Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there was an incident that you had mentioned where a Kosovo Albanian doctor or physician had been killed. Mr. Cepic asked you whether or not you had been there when it happened. You indicated no, you were there a couple of days later. How did you find out about what happened there? What was your source of information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It came out in various ways. In the first place, our KLA liaison officers had told us. Second, sort of more obviously than that, was we were actually aware that there was fighting going on along that ridge and when we were allowed to, eventually to go in, we went in and had a look, and we found a number of bodies in the field and the body at the doctor's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations with any of the Serb forces that were deployed in that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did they tell you about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I questioned -- when I raised the point that this was a medical station, they told me that as far as they're concerned that there were terrorists in that area and it was a legitimate target.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I want to go and if we could show the witness Exhibit 395. While that's coming up, Colonel Ciaglinski, Mr. Ackerman was asking you some questions about the -- the Holbrooke agreement and about the OSCE's mission to verify the cease-fire, and you will recall your discussion, I think, starting at page 6920. Yes. And there was a question. You, I think, raised the issue that you had under the terms of the various agreements you had access throughout Kosovo, and I believe Mr. Ackerman was making the point, well, the mission, though, was to verify the cease-fire, and there's no need for you to go in barracks, et cetera, to verify a cease-fire. Could we look at the next page of this exhibit. And if we could scroll down, yes, to the paragraph that's underlined. Could you read for us that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. "In order to further encourage the return to peace and normality, the state authorities of the FRY will bring down the level of presence and the equipment of security forces (MUP and VJ) throughout Kosmet to normal levels, i.e., to the levels preceding the outbreak of terrorist activities."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to the bottom of the page. It says: "With these goals in mind, the state authorities of the FRY have announced the following measures," and on the bottom of this page they talk about special police units that were deployed after February 1998 will be withdrawn. Can we go to the next page, please. Number 2: "Any additional heavy weapons or equipment brought in or transferred after February 1998 are to be withdrawn or returned from the MUP to the VJ." Number 3: "Heavy weapons and equipment remaining under MUP control will be returned to the police stations." Number 4: "All VJ units and additional equipment brought in after February 1998 will be withdrawn." And number 5 about border guards. Was this some of the kinds of things that you were trying to verify?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it necessary to go into garrisons to do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's where the equipment was kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 6947 Mr. Ivetic asked you several questions on cross-examination, and one of them had to do with the point about traffic or crime control roadblocks. To your knowledge, in Kosovo at the time what kind of uniforms did the traffic police wear?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Traffic police wore a totally different uniform which was a standard police uniform which was not combat kit but ordinary pair of trousers, a belt, and a shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And these --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And a different hat, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: These 27 points, the check-points that were discussed in the agreement, did you see traffic police at those check-points?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, the 27 points, that was the maximum number of which I think the agreement said no more than a third should be manned at any one time, i.e., 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of police were seen by the OSCE verifiers at those check-points when verifications were attempted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Heavily armed MUP police in combat equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know, were those the kind of police that were engaged in crime control?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we saw much sort of crime control going on. It was mainly sort of major operations in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If we set aside anti-terrorist, whether that's crime control or something else.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, crime control to me is quite different from anti-terrorist operations. Normally anti-terrorist operations are carried out by military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 6952, line 10 Mr. Ivetic showed you an entry from one of DZ's annexes, I think at number 8, which had a 5 January 1999 entry saying that all 27 OPs inspected, that most were occupied by the MUP. At this time in January, did you observe MUP also in addition to OPs having roving patrols?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The MUP were travelling, would be found everywhere in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did the -- did the number of those roving patrols observed by OSCE remain constant throughout or did they increase or decrease during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the MUP operations increased throughout our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 6923, line 21, there was a document shown in a reference to Mr. Nikolaev, who was described as a reconstruction man. I'm just curious, what was a reconstruction man?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see. The -- there was someone in charge of actually reconstructing Kosovo, I think building new schools or new housing developments. That's reconstruction, actually. There was a separate Deputy Head of Mission responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there was a separate one responsible for reviewing the judiciary and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You were also asked about a document that set forth some of the discussions that you were having internally in the OSCE. One of the things that was discussed was a concern about the possibility of KLA fabricating incidents. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you said -- you discussed all kinds of possibilities internally. Did you also discuss the possibility or concerns about Serbs fabricating incidents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to look at both sides and examine all possibilities and how events were -- what had happened, how they had taken place, why they were taking place, what could have been the motivation, the rationale behind them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Finally, just a last couple of questions, and I've been informed that Haeslip is spelled H-e-a-s-l-i-p.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was close.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sepenuk asked you about were you aware that General DZ had testified in Milosevic and indicated: "Nobody talked to me about the plan." Since you and DZ testified in the Milosevic case, and before testifying here, did you have any conversation with him about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- I mean, we are good friends. You know, over the years we've -- we've talked about all these issues, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- did you ever remind him, Hey, remember I told you about this plan that Kotur told me about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did he respond when you told him that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He agreed he hadn't actually told me. I told him and he -- he remembers the conversation we had about it in general because there were so many things happening, and he said it was just a possibility and it just seemed likely, unlikely, he just didn't know what to make of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no other questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave in the redirect by Mr. Hannis a new topic arose on page 24, lines 15, 16, 17, and 18. The witness mentioned something he had not mentioned before; namely, the area of Vucitrn, or south of Vucitrn. He said there was a lot of shelling and fighting, and the mission could not have access but could see the villages burn. So that's page 24, lines 15 through 18. If my memory serves me well, we did not hear these details before from the witness, and they do not feature in his statement, so I would like an opportunity to clarify these matters with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was in answer to my question explaining about training areas sometimes involved setting up a perimeter that included villages. I don't think he mentioned those specific villages or locations before, but he did address that topic, and that was a topic asked about on cross-exam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, it's something that should not be regarded as -- as normal procedure, but we shall allow you to ask a maximum of three questions to clarify what you wish to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to express my great gratitude to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ciaglinski, I already introduced myself to you and asked you some questions. Just with regard to these events south of Vucitrn. Was that in March?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that the OSCE mission was represented by Captain Ferdinand, Aleksander Lubarenko [phoen], and other persons in this matter? Were they in charge on behalf of KVM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an area that -- it was their regional area, but I and DZ had roaming rights. We could go where and see what we liked. We didn't have to ask the regional centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I hope you agreed that those villages in the direction that you were looking at were Brusnik and Bukos.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the villages to the south. I think one of them was Bukos, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I introduced one exhibit in e-court, 5D26, just relating to -- to this particular issue. Thank you again for this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I've just a brief question to clarify a position. While you were exercising your roaming rights and were keeping a vigil on these places which were being obstructed or which were being manned by people, did you wear your -- did you attire yourself in some uniform?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no uniform, sir. The only thing we had were yellow hats that we used to wear, but the most obvious thing about our presence were the bright orange vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And they were acquainted with the -- with the fact that these belonged to your organisation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone recognised the orange vehicles, and I think a lot of people at the check-points also were aware of who I was. I was referred to quite a lot by the Serbian side as Mr. Richard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Okay. The second question is there was some vagueness in the expression about the people who were attired there manning these positions, because you knew that what VJ uniform was, but these people were not attired, as you said, in the uniform of the police, and some of the insignias also you could not see because you were not so close. But please tell us, then, what sort of uniforms were these people wearing who were manning these position posts and positions. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, sir. The police had two uniforms; one was the normal working uniform that they would wear in peacetime and in -- in the headquarters; and the other one, for operational reasons, they would put on military-type combat kit. But this combat kit wasn't green. It was usually blue, sort of a mottled blue or dark blue uniform with helmets, with webbing, which is the strapping that -- which holds the ammunition belts, with boots. So they were still police, but these were police that were deployed on operations, so anti-terrorist operations as opposed to carrying out routine traffic duties, routine investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And the people you found there who were posted there while you were on your roaming exercise, they were wearing this uniform you've just described?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The MUP always wore in the field, we only saw them in military-type -- police military-type uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But police had that type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That completes your evidence, Mr. Ciaglinski. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give evidence. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Kravetz will lead the next witness. It's Gordana Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: As Mr. Hannis just indicated, the next witness is Ms. Tomasevic. I will change places over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The schedule that you've provided for forthcoming witnesses suggests that you will examine in witness for an hour. It's becoming very difficult to keep control over the time used in the course of the trial because witnesses are being presented not as originally I think generally envisaged as mainly witnesses whose evidence would be in writing or alternatively given live. It's not immediately obvious why it should be necessary to examine this witness for an hour when we have the statement and bearing in mind the nature of the evidence that's to be given.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is true. That's the estimate that was indicated in the witness notification, but I assume I'm going to be way under or well under that estimated time. I don't think I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the norm for this should be half an hour in terms of our original approach to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We -- we are proposed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- this type of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, but we are proposing this witness as a Rule 92 ter/live in the event that her evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this is a concept that really is one that you've invented as the case has progressed. All your witnesses are -- as it turns out are live because they're giving evidence by word of mouth here, and then part of their evidence is being admitted in the form of writing. But where the bulk of that evidence from a witness of this nature is given in writing, we envisaged, as our order about time-keeping indicated, that such witnesses would give live evidence for about half an hour and that if you wanted to do something different you would apply to us. I know that the rules of the Tribunal changed from this 92 bis situation to this 92 ter after the trial began, but this is the sort situation where we envisaged that you would ask us and justify needing more than half an hour to present this evidence, because if you don't do that it gives us great difficulty in controlling cross-examination and the time involved in cross-examination, and the tail's beginning to wag the dog as far as allocation of time in the trial is concerned. Now, what is about this evidence that requires more than half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see your point, and I'm going to try my best to stick to the half an hour that's usually allocated to Rule 92 ter witnesses and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And can you tell me whether there are any named witness -- any named victims related to this evidence or is this evidence of deaths which are unspecified in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In the forensic reports which we are going to seek to tender through this witness, there are approximately 12 persons who are named, 5 of whom are in -- persons who are named in our schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which schedule is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Schedule F which deals with the Izbica killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to point out before I start with this witness that in the witness notification we included the Rule 65 ter summary as filed in May of this year. Under the heading updated summary, we have included some additional paragraphs that were left out of the summary that was filed this year. I have inquired with some of my colleagues. It seems that this was just simply due to an oversight on our part, and I would seek leave to add those paragraphs back to the Rule 65 ter summary of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you understand there is no objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I haven't heard anything from the Defence with regard to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I have something else to raise. I was just waiting for Ms. Kravetz to finish because we had an agreement between us, and I thought she would sort of notify you about it. It has nothing to do with this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The query at the moment is whether there is any objection to the update to the 65 ter summary relating to this witness. Well, I see no objections so we shall allow that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the matter that Mr. Visnjic wanted to bring up, prior to commencing court today we discussed the possibility of tendering this statement, striking out one of the paragraphs. So when -- at a later stage I will indicate which one of the paragraphs we have agreed to strike out. If that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Good afternoon, Dr. Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry for talking across you as you came into the courtroom but we hadn't quite concluded a discussion preliminary to your evidence. Could you now make the some declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Gordana Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, Ms. Tomasevic, I understand that you are a forensic medicine specialist currently employed at the military medicine academy in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Since when have you been working at this institution, Ms. Tomasevic?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: From the 22nd of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Ms. Tomasevic, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution in March 2003?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 3rd and 5th March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is P2490.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you provide a second statement on 25th July, 2006, where you made some clarifications to the evidence that you had provided in your earlier statements and provided additional information?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you recently had time to review these statements and the attachment to these statements?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And having reviewed these statements, are you satisfied that the information contained in these statements accurately reflects the truth of the events that you described there to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender these two statements; these are P2490, P2507. And the first statement has a series of attachments; these are P2491 to P2499.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Will you be clarifying what these are as you progress through the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm not going to go through each of these attachments. They are explained in the written evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but how do we know which one is which as far as numbers are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I can -- yeah. I can go one by one, if you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it will be necessary, otherwise we won't know which is which.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: P2491 is Annex I to the witness statement dated March 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: P2492 is Annex II which is an order issued by investigating judge, Milutin Sekavic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is it the same all the way up to 2499 that the last number is the same as the number of the annex?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: They are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. These will be admitted. You should tell us which paragraph you're deleting from the statement, though, otherwise it will be wrongly admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was just going to do that, Your Honour. We have agreed to strike out paragraph 2 of the statement, the statement dated March 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. These statements will be admitted with that deletion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Ms. Tomasevic, in paragraph 11 and 12 of your statement of March 2003, you indicate that on 10 May 1999 you were informed that you and your colleagues were to travel to Nis and to report to the Nis military hospital to Dr. Kostic at the military hospital there. When you were provided this information, were you provided any reasons as to why you were being sent to Nis?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was just verbally informed that on the 11th of May I should report to Dr. Kostic in Nis. He was director of the military hospital in Nis, and nothing else was said. I received no other order in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 14 of the same statement you indicate that once you -- that you arrived at the Nis hospital, reported to Mr. Kostic, he indicated that you were to travel to Pristina in Kosovo but that he did not provide further information as to what would be your task in Kosovo. Was it the regular procedure for you to be sent to the field in this manner with no information as to the tasks that you were going to be carrying out?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. That was no regular procedure by any means. For that kind of job, if anybody is sending you anywhere, and especially to war, you had to have written orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm likely to appear particularly -- the word I would use but perhaps you're not familiar with is pernickety today in view of what happened yesterday afternoon. The two questions you've asked so far are clearly answered in the statement, and we really must use this time to better advantage than simply asking the witness to go over what she's clearly set out in the statement. I do, however, have a -- assuming that you've passed paragraph 12, I have a question about paragraph 12 of the statement where you say that the instruction for this came by telegram. Was that an appropriate way in which to get an instruction for this type of work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That was not the regular procedure, and I received no cable, no telegram that day. I got hold of that telegram after I came back of Kosovo in mid-June, and only because I insisted. I don't remember anymore who finally gave it to me. So initially I received no orders and no telegram about that business trip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For the avoidance of any doubt on this paragraph, the very last sentence in English says: In fact -- and this is a reference to Dr. Strbac, he had -- did you mean to say never seen a decomposed dead body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. He had not seen a decomposed dead body because he's a pathologist and I'm a forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's to clarify the use of the English language which was a problem. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Ms. Tomasevic, in your statement you referred to your arrival to Pristina, and you indicate that upon arriving you were directed to the command headquarters. Who directed you to present yourself there to the command headquarters?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. We received instructions that upon arrival in Pristina we should report to the command. We did that. The military command was located in a hotel. I don't remember the name of the hotel. And we were met by Generals Pavkovic and Lazarevic. I mean they met the whole of my team.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall what was discussed during that first meeting with Generals Pavkovic and Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing much. We just chatted. They offered us coffee and drinks and that was all for that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you referred in paragraph 16 to a second meeting that you had at the same location with General Pavkovic and Lazarevic. Do you recall who else was present during this second meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: That second meeting was on the 22nd May when we were invited to attend the military command in order to be sent to the first mission, to the first location, that is, and if I remember well there was General Dzakovic and some other officers, but I really can't tell you more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I -- can I take it that between the 12th of May and the 22nd of May you didn't just stay in Pristina? Did you go back to your normal working duties during these 10 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We were there all the time left to our own devices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Tomasevic, you indicate that during the second meeting General Pavkovic explained to you that you were going to use your expertise for the purpose of asanacija. What did you understand that he was referring to by this comment?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: He explained to us, and I gathered myself, that we were to be engaged in so-called sanitization jobs, which imply the taking of hygienic and sanitization measures, specifically collecting corpses, performing post-mortems and, if possible, identification before burial in order to prevent the spreading of contamination or infection. When the bodies have been autopsied, they are then buried into either mass or individual graves. That is the procedure that was followed both in peacetime and in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you indicate in paragraph 17 that during this meeting you received a verbal order from General Pavkovic to attend an abandoned house in a location called Staro Cikatovo. Do you recall exactly what were his instructions, what you were going to be carrying out at this location as a duty?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: He was not in a position to give any instructions except the order itself because he doesn't know what the job of a forensic pathologist is. So concerning that location, in view of the fact that I am a forensic pathologist, and I am the only one there, and I work only on the orders, written orders, of an investigating judge, and I insisted to get that order, so as to see on whose orders I'm working, he told me to that under he said, There is no order, I'm ordering you verbally. And that's how we had to go to that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you described in the -- in the following paragraphs 18 and 19 what you saw at that location. When you returned to Pristina, I understand you prepared a report based on your observations of what the -- of your findings at this location. Was this report ever handed over to General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. It cannot be. It couldn't be submitted to him because he wasn't the one who could order it. And anyway, it wasn't done by orders of the court. And anyway, General Pavkovic did not ask for the report from that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did anyone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Doctor, where is the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those reports, I don't know if they are still in existence. I used to have them. They were written and they were signed complete with photo documentation that I received at my own personal request some years ago, but where they are I really don't know. That -- what matters is that I didn't submit them to anybody.
