utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. I understand that matters to you and why, but what matters to us more importantly is what it's in them. Has no one ever asked you to try to trace the report? The Prosecutor, did they ask you before coming to try and trace this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. Nobody asked for reports from that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Has a letter of request been sent to the government of Serbia for this report?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, the witness has never handed the report over to local -- any local authorities, and it was my understanding that the report is no longer in her possession, but maybe the witness can clarify this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did you do with the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right now I really don't know where those reports are, whether I destroyed them, maybe, but I doubt that. I wrote the report up then in 1999 when I came back. I was hoping that somebody would ask for them but nobody did. And the reports were not done on the orders of the court. I, as a forensic pathologist, had no one to give them to. So the only thing that could have happened is that they stayed with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you can't remember whether you still have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it might have been a good idea to ask the witness to have a look before she came, but there we go, it's too late now. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I know a request for assistance was made with regard to the other reports, and we do have those in our possession.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you indicate that you were tasked with three further examinations, and I want to direct your attention to the examinations that you performed on 101 bodies that were brought from Izbica in Srbica municipality. I understand from your written evidence that you personally did not attend the exhumations that were carried out at this location at Izbica but that your colleague, Dr. Strbac, was present. Do you recall what information he provided, if any, regarding these exhumations that were carried out in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: We did not discuss that. He just told me that the graves were individual, the bodies were buried individually. That was all. We didn't talk about that anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Tomasevic, I understand that the bodies were brought from Izbica in trucks to locations in Kosovska Mitrovica where you carried out the examinations. At what location specifically did you carry out this examination?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: On the first day, on 3rd June, we tried to perform external examinations, that is autopsies, in an area next to the hospital in Kosovska Mitrovica. However, the conditions were very bad. The place was very narrow, teeming with flies, and then we decided to do it in a hangar also in Kosovska Mitrovica. So we continued to perform the autopsies in that hangar for three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And other than your team who else was present during these examinations in this hangar?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the members of my team, this was attended as specified in the order of the investigating judge, scene of crime technicians from the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica, and men from the so-called utilities company; also from Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, did you prepare an individual report for each one of these bodies that you examined at this location?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit P248 be brought up in e-court. Could I have the English version here. Could we zoom in on the -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Ms. Tomasevic?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I wrote up these autopsy protocols as they're called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Ms. Tomasevic, I see that the date on this report is 3rd June 1999. You indicated, however, in your statement of July of this year that all the reports have the same dates but that your examinations were carried out in a period of three days, from 3rd to 5th June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like to add that I did not turn over my autopsy protocols to the investigating judge. Instead, on the 30th December 2003, for completely different reasons I turned them over for safekeeping to the first municipal court in Belgrade. How they landed here, I don't understand. They are quite incomplete, and they have not been signed by me. And I would also like to point out to certain errors that exist in every protocol.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. You indicated that there are some errors in this protocol. Could you tell us what those errors are that you would have liked to correct at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that. First of all, the most important error that is the greatest concern to you -- let me first explain why I made these mistakes. I did this in 1999 when I made the first autopsy protocol. I just numbered the other ones by copying and pasting the reference number. So the mistakes were copied. I said that they were attended, the post-mortems were attended by military police members, which is not true. They were attended by civilian police. The military police had nothing to do with it. Then I said the photographing was done by Ivica Jovanovic, because that was the only name that I could remember. Instead, I should have said scene of crime officers from the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica. Third mistake, the descriptions of damage on clothing is missing, and this damage is not compared to the wounds and injuries on the body. The -- another mistake is that the date is wrong. The date is the same on all protocols, and they were in fact done over three days. The bodies were brought in black bags, and since they were exhumed by excavator certain damage was inflicted on the bodies in the course of excavations. So I described such damage as defects rather than injuries. Those are the major mistakes. In other terms, I would not change anything to these protocols.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think we're having a problem with e-court. I can't seem to get an English -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll have our break at this stage. Doctor, we have to break at this time each day and we break for about 20 minutes or so. While we have this break, you need to leave the courtroom. So could you go with the usher and he will show you where to wait and we'll see you in about 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have page 3 of the -- this exhibit up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Ms. Tomasevic, you have a section called "Conclusions" in front of you, on the screen in front of you. Could we zoom in on that, please. Thank you. Ms. Tomasevic, in this section under the heading "Conclusion," you state that the corpse -- that in this case the corpse that you examined was in an advanced state of putrefaction and that the time and cause of death could not be determined with reliability, but it was possible to confirm the wounds. And in the second paragraph you say that the wounds on the corpse were to the trunk probably inflicted by projectiles from -- it says in the English "side-arms." I believe this is a typo; it should say "fire-arms." Ms. Tomasevic, from what you could observe on these bodies, were most of the bodies have this type of injuries that you assumed were from fire-arms, or is this case that we're looking at now an exception?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. The bodies or, rather, the people were probably killed by projectiles fired from fire-arms, as far as I can recall. With one corpse we had a blunt injury, whereas all the others were probably killed by fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, based on your observations did most of these -- were most of these bodies dressed in civilian clothes or did you also find bodies dressed in any -- some sort of uniform, either a complete uniform or part of a uniform?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The bodies were in civilian clothes for the most part. There were several bodies in black KLA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, before the break you indicated to us some corrections that you would have liked to make, or some errors that are contained in these reports. If you had had the time would you have also modified these conclusions or do these conclusions reflect accurately your findings as to the examinations that you conducted on these bodies?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't change the conclusions. The conclusions contain everything I could -- all the conclusions I could come to after the autopsy. As for the other facts concerning the existing wounds characteristics based on which I concluded that they probably resulted from gunshot -- from fire-arms injuries, and as for the trajectory canals and due to the fact that many injuries result from such canals and from entry/exit wounds as well as the comparison between the damage to the clothes and the injuries, the number of injuries, the sequence of injuries as well as the mechanism which caused the injuries, as well as concerning the information on which of those injuries were the result of death, all of those facts could be addressed by me only as an expert, but as someone who carried out an autopsy, I produced these conclusions. This is all I could do in that capacity. For such type of information, I would have had to have received another order from the investigative judge to clarify. As a forensic pathologist, I usually receive an order from the investigative judge to carry out a forensic autopsy. After that, I make conclusions on the cause of death, and I state what weapon was used, whether it was a fire-arm or blunt instrument. I put that in my conclusions, and I forward the report to the investigative judge. Then the investigative judge needs to draft another report for an expert examination, and he can task me or another forensic pathologist with doing that. In case of fire-arm injuries, the investigative judge would request information from the expert on the cause of death. This would include the instrument used, the sequence of injuries, and the injuries which caused death and all the aforementioned factors. I also need to categorise the injuries as well as the mechanism behind them, as well as to specify the type of weapons used. As for the latter, I would need a ballistics expert for that. A forensic pathologist does not make conclusions as to the types of weapons used to cause injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, very briefly, I understand that some of these body-bags in which the bodies were brought contained some wooden grave markers that were found at the site in Izbica, and these markers indicated the names of some of these persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. During the exhumation, in certain graves we found wooden markers which resembled small ladders, pieces of wood with Albanian names on them. All such markers were put in bags together with the bodies and transported to Kosovska Mitrovica, and I noted that in my autopsy reports. I believe only a few bodies had such markers. This was noted in the paragraph pertaining to clothing. For example, I can't see it in this report, but when describing clothing, after that the next sentence would be "Together with the body there is a marker being forwarded with a specific name engraved." This is as much as I can recall, and it was only in several cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand from your -- your written evidence that you concluded these examinations on 5th June 1999. Did you carry out any further taskings while in Kosovo after you completed the Izbica examinations?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. We left Kosovo on the 14th of June. In the period between the 5th and the 14th of June we were also left to our devices, and we didn't do much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these reports that you prepared on the basis of your examinations were never -- you told us you -- they were never handed to local authorities at the time. Were you ever paid for them at any later stage, for these examinations that you conducted?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was never paid for it. I have knowledge from my sources who were close to the then government who told me that the then minister of justice and minister of finance told me that -- that they wouldn't pay a penny. I was told by their own assistants never to hand over the documentation until I receive my fee. I have my attorney working on it, my lawyer, and this procedure is still pending. It is still before our courts, and I have believe and I hope that it will be resolved soon. I also wanted to state that I never asked an apartment or a rank or a promotion for the job I did. This would have been far better for me, but I only wanted to receive what I was due according to the criminal law and laws of our country.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You stated earlier that you later left these reports in custody at a court. In which court did you leave these reports in custody? Where exactly?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: It was the First District Court in Belgrade. As I said, I learned from some people who were highly positioned then and who were members for the National Committee for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal that they tried to state that I wasn't in possession of such information whatever, and although they knew I had it because I was on the spot, there was also a criminal report submitted against me by Mr. Svilanovic for the offence of obstruction of evidence. First of all, I wanted to show that I had that documentation. Second of all, I have my lawyer working on it to who advised me to hand the documentation over so as to prove that I indeed have it. I deposited it with the First Belgrade Court in December 2003. I handed over the complete documentation, including photographs, which was subsequently forwarded by the crime scene technicians who had taken them. Those people were from the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Those are all my questions for this witness, Your Honour. I wish to tender Exhibit P248, which is this collection of forensic autopsies for the Izbica bodies. And I wish to point out to Your Honours, as I indicated earlier, there are five named victims in our schedule that are referred to in these reports. Maybe I could indicate the number of the forensic report just to facilitate reference at a further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So this is number 55. It's Mr. Bekir Musliu. Number 83, Ali Dragaj. Number 84, Asim Osmani. Number 88 is Istric Srepmali [phoen]. And number 93 is Simber Shala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the means of identification of these as victims here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You mean the names in the forensic reports or the evidence we have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. How is it that you identify that these bodies examined by this witness included these five named persons?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: There -- there were witnesses who have testified before this court already with regard to Izbica have provided evidence as to the identity of these persons. For example, I can give you one example, concrete example, is number 83, Ali Dragaj. We have evidence from Witness Mustafa Dragaj who names him as being present in his group of persons in Izbica when these killing incidents took place. There's also evidence from Ms. -- Dr. Liri Loshi who filmed the bodies as you will probably recall in Izbica on -- in the aftermath of after these events, and Ali Dragaj's body actually is shown on the photograph. They're attached to his statement and the video that we tendered through Mr. Liri Loshi, and you will see his body has a name tag with his name and the information concerning date of birth, which corresponds to what is in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that the basis for linking the autopsies to the victims, that the victim had a name tag, as it were, in -- along with the body?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. And as the witness just indicated and has also explained in her statement, some of the bodies came -- the body-bags had wooden plates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I'm referring to. Are all five that you've named here, do they fall into that category?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. The person I referred to, Ali Dragaj, I think he had his identity card in his pocket and so that's how he was identified by Ms. Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does that apply to the other four, that it's that kind of identification that's being done here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's identification either because they have the documents on them at the time they were examined by Ms. Tomasevic or the wooden plate with the name which was put at the burial site was included in the body-bag which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can -- can I ask you a question about paragraph 67 and 68 of the statement of the -- of March 2003? Are these two paragraphs part of the letter?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is part of the exhibit, of the attachment to this statement. It's not clear from the -- from the way it's been included here in this statement, but this is part of the attachment to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And P248 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will follow the indictment in this case, and the Milutinovic Defence has no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Tomasevic. I have a few questions for you. The first topic I want to deal with concerns your departure to Kosovo. I would kindly ask the Registrar to put P2491 on e-court. It is a telex --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: -- sent to Mr. Spasic by Mr. Krgovic. The penultimate sentence of the document reads: "The transport and travel will be carried out pursuant to orders of the administration of the VMA." Page 2, please. The part written by hand has two sentences. The sentence number two says: "The order is issued by the VMA administration." Do you know of this order?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. I've never seen it. As I stated previously, I managed to retrieve the telegram in mid-June, I believe. If I returned on the 14th of June, it must have been around the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Concerning that and paragraph 12 of your first statement, this being P2490, you say that when you came to the VMA you said you were told that civilians do not receive orders but only military officers, and Mr. Strbac was appointed as head of the team, and he was an officer.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In your July statement, you clarify that on the 10th of May you were called by Major Strbac and he told you to report to the military hospital in Nis. And then you said: "I don't know where the order received on Mr. Strbac originated from, where it came from."

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The next topic has to do with the Staro Cikatovo location. In paragraph 18 of your statement from 2003, you state that you were taken to the house by some soldiers, and once you arrived some 300 metres away you heard machine-gun fire. As relating -- relates to that, in paragraph 20 you say: "There is no evidence based on which an identification could have been carried out, and the autopsies were not carried out because of the conditions there." And my question was: What were the conditions?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say it was machine-gun fire. I do not have such knowledge of weaponry. That was the way it was interpreted. I said I heard bursts of gunfire. Second of all, you being a lawyer should know that an autopsy should not and must not be done in wartime, in war conditions, and nowhere in the world do you see autopsies carried out during combat activities. They occur only after the signing of truce. It is only in the territory of the former Yugoslavia that the military academy teams engaged in such risky jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tomasevic. As opposed to the other three locations you testified on, the Staro Cikatovo location saw no exhumation and no autopsy. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: You're not. There was no exhumation because the bodies were in an abandoned house. The external examination I carried out would equal carrying out autopsy in peacetime and it was wartime there. I also made some dental examinations, something I didn't do in the other locations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel and witness should pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you just bear with me a moment. Because you're speaking the same language the interpreters have difficulty keeping up with your pace. It's important that when Mr. Aleksic finishes his question you wait and just to allow the interpretation to catch up. You'll see from the screen in front of you when it runs out. Now, could you start that answer again, please, if you remember the question clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember what the question was. There was no exhumation because the bodies were in an abandoned house, and this was probably repeated when I was giving my interpretation and must be in my statement when I said that autopsies are not carried out in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards that, you said that the military crime scene technicians photographed the site. On page 43, line 18, 19 and further on, you stated that you received the photographs from that location?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, upon my insistence. I received it from Leskovac some two years ago, I believe. I received all the photographs of the spot and the bodies. I didn't have them back in March 2003, although I do have them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how and from whom you received the documentation?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I have the official letter which accompanied it. My security officers from the VMA are familiar with that. I -- I sent out a request to someone in Leskovac and I received that from Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Does this pertain to the military judiciary or the military police bodies?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In any case, it pertains to the military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: After this event in Staro Cikatovo you were in contact with the investigating judges of the military court affiliated to the command of the Pristina Corps with regard to the next locations?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The next locations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In those communications did you mention this report and the location of Staro Cikatovo?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: When you came back to your employer, the military medical academy, did you inform any of your superiors or the chief of your section, your supervisor?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course I informed my then chief, Dr. Zoran Stankovic. I tried to get hold of information because he's a man of great experience with wartime and war conditions, and he told me that he would not be standing behind me. He would not be supporting me. He's absolutely not interested in my protocols, and he would not place his signature on my protocols as my supervisor, nor would he allow the seal of the institute of forensic medicine to be placed on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me during your stay in Pristina were you in contact with the chief of the sanitary service of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't even know who that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just two more questions. During the examination-in-chief, you spoke about sanitization and the notion of sanitization as explained by General Pavkovic, and you said that this job involves taking steps necessary for identification of bodies and establishing the cause of death. My question is: Everything that you and your team did in May and June in Kosovo had to do with steps to identify the bodies and establish the cause of death; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: My job was to perform post-mortems, plus identification only if the latter is possible, and we have to know that this was wartime. Identification is possible only with the attendance of family members. But if we were dealing with unidentified corpses, that is not possible, and we were dealing with unidentified corpses in my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: But you did take all the other steps towards that objective?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Which objective?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you said your job involved taking steps to perform post-mortems and identify the bodies and establish the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I read my statement, and I saw that sentence. I think that is something that is implied when the investigating judge writes his order. He writes the order, and then it's a matter of course that the pathologist should try to identify the body. But if there is no family, if there are no friends, then the burial is performed by the utilities company of that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's me. Thank you, Your Honour. I do apologise. I do have a problem with the earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. My name is Djuro Cepic, attorney-at-law. I'd like to ask you a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'll try to speak a little more slowly, which is unusual for our language, but that is all for the benefit of the interpreters. You mentioned that upon arrival in Kosovo you had two meetings with Generals Pavkovic and Lazarevic. Those meetings were attended by a number of persons. Can you tell me: Apart from the team that you led, were those meetings attended by some other teams or members of teams?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No, just my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And do you know that at that time in Kosovo, apart from the team that you led, there were any other expert teams?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: You mean from the military academy in Belgrade or Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Tell me first about the military medical academy.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I remember that before I departed Dr. Stankovic was there. How long he stayed, I don't know. When he came back another team left led by the present chief, Dr. Milosavljevic, together with pathologist Kosta from Nis. I saw him only on the first day when I arrived on the 12th of May, and I know that he had some health problems and General Lazarevic gave him permission to leave, and he did not come back again. So we spent all of 34 days there, which is absolutely inhuman, because teams are relieved every 10 days normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understand. I see that from your statement. I'll try to put my questions concisely and I would appreciate similar answers. This conversation that you had with General Pavkovic, is it correct that he asked you to do your best in keeping with the rules of your profession, to perform all the required activities?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't ask any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So it was an informal conversation.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we arrived on the 12th of May. He explained that as a medical expert team we were supposed to do the sanitization of terrain, and I confirmed to him that I understood the term "sanitization" in that way. And before I left I consulted with Professor Dunjic, who was my greatest and only teacher, and he also had explained to me before what sanitization meant, and General Pavkovic is not familiar with forensic medicine, so he wasn't able to tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That was precisely going to be my next question. He is not competent to tell you what you --

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Of course he's not competent to tell me what I'm supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Far from that. Let us come back to Staro Cikatovo. On that occasion, there were military investigating bodies present?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No, just soldiers or officers. Nothing like an investigating judge. There was scene-of-crime officers from the military, yes, but not military investigators, if you mean the investigating judge or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Please allow me. This is my field of expertise as it happens. Even scene-of-crime officers belong with the military investigating bodies.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But as a lawyer, you know that I'm supposed to work only on orders of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Of course I know that.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Makes me very happy to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that there is documentation from this site? You said that it was only in 2003 that you got it at your own insistence.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say anything about 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You explicitly said in response to questions by -- questions by Mr. Aleksic that it was only in March 2003 that you got documentation from the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: March 2003. I'm not aware of that. You must not have been listening. I don't know when I got it. Maybe two or three years ago, but nothing about March 2003. If I had known that, I would also have known from whom I had received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Doctor. Do you know that all this material taken over by military investigating bodies was deposited and turned over to the court, military court during combat actions and they still have a copy?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Which military court and which documentation? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Documents related to Staro Cikatovo, the time you spent there, the work you did there, the protocols, the photographs, everything that was done was turned over under the Law on Criminal Procedure to the --

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my documents were not turned over to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We're not talking about your documents. I'm talking about the on-site investigation report, the photo documentation from the site.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I have all that. I've said that. I got it -- I got that material at my own request. The on-site investigation report and the photo file relating to that site and the bodies, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you are aware that exist -- that it existed from the very first moment.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Of course it existed. There were people there who photographed every body. I as a forensic pathologist have the obligation to have every corpse photographed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That is your obligation in relation to the corpses, and as we have seen - I'll try to speak more slowly - in your Exhibit P248 every corpse was photographed four or five times, and those photographs make an integral part of your autopsy reports.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: From what I remember, I have only one photograph per corpse in the material I got from Leskovac, not four or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about the autopsy reports from Izbica?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: In those I have more per body; several hundred photographs in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank -- I thank the interpreters. I am indeed sorry for speaking too fast. Let us clarify one more point, Doctor. It is your obligation to get pictures of the bodies, but according to the letter of the Law on Criminal Procedure and in keeping with the rules of your profession, you need photographs for your own expertise and other photographs regarding exhumation and other relevant affairs are the responsibility of scene-of-crime technicians and they are probably turned over to investigating judges?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I never get exhumation photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was one dilemma concerning your statement because you said you did not receive those photographs.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: On the contrary. I think I said in my statement that it was not unusual at all for me not to get pictures from the exhumations. You should have read it more carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I read it carefully.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I said it was not at all unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let me just check that everything is correctly recorded in the transcript, that everything that has been said is in the transcript. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Page 64, line 4, unfortunately due to the speed of this exchange, it's not the whole answer. The answer is: "Thank you. I never got scene-of-crime photographs." However, the real answer was a bit longer, considerably longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I doubt if it's going to assist us very much, Mr. Cepic, to know any more than we've already got from the witness on this matter. We seem to be diverted from the essence of her evidence at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you mentioned in your statement those two sites, Belo Polje, municipality of Pec, and Malo Ribare village in Lipljan. There everything was done in keeping with the rules of your profession, science and the provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. The investigating judge attend on both locations, as should have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And all your activities in Kosovo performed during the bombing and combat operations were extremely risky. On a couple of occasions you were exposed, you were under fire?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I was constantly under fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So you suffered?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Lots.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know maybe -- [In English] I do apologise. [Interpretation] Do you know perhaps that during the exhumation of bodies in Izbica locality of which we have heard quite a great deal now there were even some terrorist activities directed at the site but also in the broader area of that location in a wide ring secured by the army of Yugoslavia? There were combat operations there that made the exhumation work considerably more difficult.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: You can do without the "even," because it went on 24 hours a day. There were no air-raid alarms like in Belgrade, because it went on non-stop. You're under fire non-stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you know that in this whole area Izbica, Drenica there were constant attacks while the exhumation was going on, while the army was holding that ring around the broader area?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just two more questions. Did you know that the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia in 2001 established the commission whose task was to gather materials about the sanitization performed in Kosovo, sanitization of the terrain performed in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I know that the General Staff did have a commission. I think its name was Commission for Cooperation with the ICTY, and I had one interview with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know, perhaps, or do you have any knowledge about the report sent to that commission of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia dated 15th May 2001, from the Institute for Forensic Pathology and Medicine, and that includes your strictly confidential report, 300-3 dated 14th May 2001?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date or the year. If you mean the report that I had to make to indicate all the locations where I worked in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was supposed to be strictly confidential, and then my name was published in a weekly with a wide circulation, thanks to Ivan Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We'll discuss it.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: You mean who gave my name for publishing?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No doubt we will be hearing more about this commission set up by the General Staff of the army on what basis it was and what work it did in due course. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will be brief, I do have just a couple questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My name is Dan Ivetic, and I am of the attorneys for Mr. Lukic, and as I indicated I have just a few questions for you. Now, first of all, Dr. Tomasevic, during your career and the over -- from what I've read you've performed over 700 forensic post-mortem inspections. For each of those instances during your career, am I correct that upon completion and submission of your report to the judicial authorities that would enable the judicial authorities to continue with their investigations and ask for any additional forensic work to be done on the bodies? Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we can -- if we can focus just on Izbica, the examination undertaken at Izbica. At paragraph 12 of your 2003 statement, you indicated for the other forensic autopsies that you took part in at Staro Cikatovo that Dr. Strbac as an officer was the head of the team, even though you clearly had more experience. Was this also the case with Izbica, that he was the formal head of the -- of the team, even though you were actually the person with the more experience in terms of doing this type of forensic work?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Strbac actually had no experience. He's just a pathologist, and that's a completely different speciality.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And am I correct that as part of your course -- post-mortem examinations of the bodies recovered from Izbica that you are unable to determine the actual time of death for any of the bodies? And when I say "you," I mean the examinations either conducted personally by you or the examinations conducted by Dr. Strbac that you oversaw.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I have no -- no sufficient parameters to be able to say anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I just have to slow down and wait for the translation to come in on the English so we don't get ahead of the translators. Based upon your knowledge and experience, Doctor, although you could not determine the time of death, did the bodies that you examined from Izbica show a similar state of decomposition or were some of the bodies showing a more advanced state of decomposition than others?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: They were all in the same state of decomposition; that is, advanced putrefaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and based upon your knowledge and experience, am I accurate to state that the -- with that state of decomposition it is almost impossible to determine the time of death based upon just the type of inspection that you carried out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that. You've already answered that question. That gives counsel the information he wants on the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you talked about some. Bodies having grave markers that accompanied the body-bags that were apparently found at the exhumation site. Do you recall that any of the bodies that you personally dealt with had grave markers that also had insignia or markings for the UCK on them?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "had insignia"? You mean on the uniforms? They had no tatoos. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've already had evidence that some of the bodies were dressed in black KLA uniforms. Do you need more than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. I'm not asking about uniforms. I'm asking about the wooden grave markers themselves, and my next question will make it obvious why I'm asking that. I can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, your report, P248, with respect to the forensic review of these bodies, I have gone through the report, and I have found five bodies that had wooden grave marks that accompanied the bodies that are reported according to your report as having some writing on -- some marking on the grave marker showing that the deceased individual was a member of the UCK, that it had an UCK symbol on the actual grave marker. Now, my question deals with whether you actually recall handling any bodies that had these wooden grave markers that accompany the bodies that also had the symbol UCK on the grave marker, and then we'll get to the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I remember that UCK was written on the tombstones.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... alert us to the fact that this report is not complete, not official, and did have some errors in it. That information being understood, I'd like to ask you specifically with respect to the descriptions of what the -- the bodies were wearing in terms of the clothing, are the descriptions of the clothing accurate so that if -- for instance, for these five individuals that had UCK grave stones, if the descriptions for these individuals show that they were wearing civilian clothes, is that actually what you saw or is that one of the errors that you had? That is to say, does the report accurately reflect what the bodies were wearing in each instance?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My report does reflect it accurately. The bodies that had grave markers marked UCK had uniforms, not civilian clothes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Tomasevic, for your time and your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you got the answer -- I think you should read the answer, Mr. Ivetic, and tell me if in fact you understand that to be what you anticipated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The translation came out a little differently. Let me ask -- let me ask the question this way:

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can -- Dr. Tomasevic, can we rely upon the descriptions of what various bodies were wearing that are contained in your -- in your protocols, your post-mortem protocols? That is to say, the descriptions of what various bodies were wearing, is that part of your report at least complete and accurate?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did my best to describe the clothing precisely, and every detail of the clothing can be clearly seen on the photographs attached to the original report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just for your information, Doctor, the reason I ask is because the photographs are not attached to this copy of the report. So that's why I needed to clarify that with you. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I'm finished with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, there is one question affecting you that arises from the way in which the cross-examination was conducted. The witness said various things about a Major-General Stankovic not supporting her, and in light of that answer the deletion of paragraph 2 is a bit unrealistic. Now, is there something --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not understand that in the context of paragraph 2. Lending support does not necessarily have to do with paragraph 2. It could be one of the possible explanations but not the only one. In my view it's not the right explanation, but I'm not going into that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem is that I'm about to ask a question about paragraph 2 and I wanted your observations before I did so, and it only the -- it arises outs of this cross-examination, but -- because I'm about to seek clarification of that very point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My comment would be that we had agreed with the Prosecutor that paragraph 2 be deleted from the statement. Now it's up to you to accept or not to accept that, but it has been our agreement from the beginning to delete paragraph 2 as irrelevant to her testimony, and I believe that regardless of what the witness has said, paragraph 2 is not relevant. But maybe I would reserve the right to ask the witness something then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with this paragraph, I think. Ms. Kravetz, do you have any comment to make?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: As Mr. Visnjic has indicated, he approached me before court and we had agreed that, as he had requested, this paragraph would be omitted, but I don't have any preference. So if Your Honour wants to reinstate this paragraph and keep it in, we had only done it to accommodate Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In view of the position taken by the Prosecution, we will leave paragraph 2 of the statement out of account. Ms. Kravetz, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have a few questions relating to medical jurisprudence. I just want to ask, did you find rigor mortis on any of the bodies present or not? Rigor mortis.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: In this -- when would you think rigor mortis would relax? Or when will it set in, when in a case in hand, I mean in the area in hand and keeping in view that weather?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is for an expert is to say; whereas, I appear here only as witness. Therefore, I cannot respond to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You're not an expert on medical jurisprudence? You have said that, that you're not a mere pathologist, you're much more. You have a degree.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I am a forensic pathologist, an expert in the field, and that was my role in the job done, where however my role here is as a witness, which is different as an expert. I can respond to your question, provided I was here in the capacity of an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Doctor, the distinction you make between an expert and someone who has actually carried out the work in a particular case is one we recognise, but at the same time a person who has carried out work on a particular case can use his or her expertise to draw conclusions which may assist us. We're not in a position now to go back to the situation where a further order might be made and an expert brought in to provide additional information. We can only rely on you as the person here with the maximum knowledge about this particular investigation. So we would be grateful if you would do your best in the circumstances to answer the questions that are put to you by Judge Chowhan. If you feel that you are not in a position because you don't have enough information to answer a question, please tell us that, but don't rely in this instance on the legalistic distinction between what you were doing and the work of an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: When you conduct an autopsy, then you observe a body. And when you observe a body, you write down a report, and that report is called the inquest report, the inquest report. And you prepare the inquest report to record your observations as you saw the body. This is universal. And then you -- you then use the knife or wherever it is required to cut the body for post-mortem examination, and then you see what you found inside the body. Now, please tell me, did you prepare the inquest report of these corpses that you saw and recorded what you saw and also recorded the condition of the body, putrefication, blueness, eating by the insects, how much of the body was left, whether it was totally eaten up or only the bones were left, or whether it had all the bones, whether it did not have certain bones, whether there was ligature mark or whether there was no ligature mark? We find that this report of yours, whatever was brought here, is destitute of that sufficient information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have to interrupt at this point. I don't agree with Judge Chowhan on this, but -- so we need to consult briefly on this again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, while we may not agree on what questions are entirely appropriate in the circumstances, Judge Chowhan does have questions he wishes to ask and he will proceed now to ask you these questions. So far you've heard what he's asked. Are you able to comment on that before he goes further?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours -- may I continue? You said that before I used the scalpel, the knife to do the internal examination, it is specified in all my reports that I conducted an external examination. I didn't go inside the body. I didn't study the cavities. An autopsy is one thing, and making an expert report is a different thing by law in my country, otherwise, I would speculating. I kindly ask you to take that into account. If the case is different in your country, then I should have been proofed on that. I should have been told that in your system there is no distinction between a witness and an expert. I can assist you, though, in saying -- or suggesting the following, since you said you were short of time: I can tell you that according to -- or pursuant a ruling on your part I can put that in writing in a relatively short time. I can make an expert report, and I can only reiterate that I cannot answer to questions which could be -- or should be posed of an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This explanation does help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid it hasn't helped me. I'm now confused about the situation. What is it you're saying, is something you cannot deal with today?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Today or tomorrow I cannot address matters that would require an expert. An expert needs to compile a report based on what he or she saw and based on facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what -- how do you define an expert?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: An expert, it is a forensic pathologist in this case, and once the forensic pathologist receives an order from the investigative judge to carry out the expertise, he has before him a -- a report compiled by either that expert or another expert. He also says -- has the complete set of documentation that was in the possession of the investigative judge containing the information on the event, the Official Note on the crime-scene investigation conducted together with a sketch of the scene, the photographs, the report from the investigation as well as various witness statements or any statement of possible defendant and data on the deceased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not being asked to reach conclusions based on that sort of material. You're being asked very limited questions about your own observations, not about anything else, and I find it difficult to see what difference it would make if you had more time to deal with this. If all that the Bench wish is further information about your findings, why can you not give us that information?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I've explained already, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, all you've said is that if someone in Serbia wrote out an order asking you to do a further report on the information you've already gathered, then you could do that as an expert. Or have I misunderstood that?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Once I received an order for autopsy, I do that. When I receive an order for expertise, I do the other one. These are two completely different matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But as I understand it, they may both be based on exactly the same information.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: When carrying out an autopsy, all you have is the body, no other data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we're only asking for information based on your observation of the body, that's all.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: All of that is contained in the conclusions. Based on the autopsy performed, I concluded that the putrefaction was advanced and that the time and cause of death cannot be established, whereas in the course of expertise I could have stipulated the possible causes of death. In item 2, I stated that the wounds in various parts of the body were most likely caused by fire-arm projectiles. Based on the parameters, I could see characteristics of the wounds, the existence of trajectory canals and so on and so forth. Once the autopsy had been carried out, I may mention the cause of death in the course of expertise, but as far as the autopsy goes, it contains what I had already mentioned. If the investigative judge is interested in obtaining more data, he needs to forward a request for expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have taken some time to consider whether we have adequate information from you on the basis of which you are prepared to give your evidence and we're now satisfied that we do, and therefore on the questions that were concerning Judge Chowhan, we do not require to ask any further questions. Judge Nosworthy wishes to deal with two quite separate matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge. With your permission, I really, Dr. Tomasevic, have just one question for you. On your statement of the 5th of March, at paragraph 54, you spoke about travel to Kosovska Mitrovica daily from Pristina through Vucitrn - please forgive my pronunciation - which was a Siptar Kosovo Albanian stronghold and dangerous to drive through. And you further said: "One day we were driving in a convoy when we were stopped and advised that communications from NATO planes had just been intercepted, and they believe that our convoy was about to be targeted." What I want to discover from you is who was it who told you that and gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: When we were approaching that area, there were soldiers and officers around. The convoy consisted of four vehicles. I remember that ours was a red Mercedes. They stopped us, and they said that thanks to our pilots, who knew the English language and who overheard NATO pilots, they learned that our convoy was about to be bombed. The area was otherwise empty. It was a clearing. Our four cars were very visible, and we would have been an easy target. So we left the vehicles and hid under some trees for about two hours until the danger was gone. And on that day --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last thing she said. Somebody was hurt, but the interpreter didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The very last part of your answer was not picked up by the interpreter. You said you left the vehicles, hid under some trees for about two hours until the danger was gone, and you went on to say something else. It started, "And on that day."

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: And later that day we found out that on the same day Daniel Shifer was injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And just to be precise, soldiers of -- I'm sorry. My microphone wasn't active. Just to be precise, soldiers of which particular army?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Our army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: "Our"?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I mean our army, the army, the troops that were in Kosovo. That was the only army, our army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And when you say "officers," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, military officers. All of them were officers. I don't know what our contract soldiers as opposed to others and I'm a medical doctor, I don't know anything about ranks. All these people were in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, who is Daniel Shifer?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what position he held, but he spent some time in our country. A Frenchman that held some position in Kosovo. He was widely known, but I really can't recall now what his title was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. That completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will break now and we will resume a bit earlier than would otherwise have been the case. We resume at five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Dragulev.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is K81. And the witness's evidence pertains to paragraphs 72 and 77 of the indictment. We are calling him pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the time you're likely to occupy in examining him?

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: I don't think I'll be more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, sir. You are known to us as K81. You realise that, I hope. So when we do not use your name, we do not mean any discourtesy to you. Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. So the Trial Chamber Judges already have your statement so we have a considerable amount of information already. You're here so that counsel for the various parties can ask some questions, to clarify points in the statement, perhaps add to them, and in some instances perhaps to challenge what you've said. The important thing is to concentrate on the particular question that's asked of you and try to confine the answer you give to the particular point that is raised in the question. The first counsel to ask questions will be for the Prosecution, and that is Ms. Dragulev.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask the usher to deliver to the witness what will be marked Exhibit P2485, the identification sheet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Mr. K81, can you please review the document that was placed in front of you and confirm that it correctly reflects your name, your date of birth, and your place of birth, without reading them out loud? Please just answer verbally with yes or no. Does it reflect your name, your place of birth, and your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to tender Exhibit P2485 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That will be done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Mr. K81, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 30th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Did you make some corrections to the statement on the 1st of February, 2002?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: During our proofing session, did you have a chance to review those statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Did you make some corrections or -- or clarifications and discover some translation errors in your statements during the proofing session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes. There were some minor mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would quickly like to go through these corrections with the witness and would ask the usher to deliver to the witness an Albanian translation of his statement. It contains numbered paragraphs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Mr. K81, you made a correction to page 1, paragraph 4 of your statement. The last sentence of that paragraph reads: "I think there were about 80 buses that brought them in." What correction did you make to that paragraph, to that sentence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: When I gave the statement, I said 8 to 10 buses, not 80 buses. This was the correction I made.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next correction was to paragraph 5 of the statement, the next paragraph. You made a correction to the sentence: "They were un-kept." You said that you did not remember saying that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I don't remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 11 of the statement, we discovered a discrepancy between the English version and the Albanian version of the statement. The third sentence of paragraph 11 reads: "We could see them from where we were in the mountains." Whereas the Albanian version states: "We could see the houses from where we were in the mountains." Which version is correct, the Albanian one or the English one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: The Albanian version is correct where it says that we could see them looting the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: That would be the English version that refers to them, "we could see them from where we were in the mountains."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the same paragraph you also made a clarification. You said that you could only see them, the people, or the villagers, through binoculars from where you were in the mountains. By using binoculars; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the same paragraph, in paragraph 11, in the Albanian version of your statement one the names that is mentioned there is spelled as Mehmeti, M-e-h-m-e-t-i. Is that the correct name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No. That's not the correct name. It should be Mahmuti.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Could you spell that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes. M-a-h-m-u-t-i.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. You then made a correction to the last sentence or in fact the last word of paragraph 15 to the part that reads: "Valbona is in the USA." What was the correction you made to the sentence? Where was Valbona at the time you gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: She was in France. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Paragraph 22 there is a reference to Fazli. You corrected that --

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour. There was a reference to the name Fazli Rustemi.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And you corrected that name to Fazli Ukshini; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's Fazli Ukshini.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Do you spell Ukshini, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: U-k-s-h-i-n-i.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And I believe the last direction was to paragraph 23 was rather translation error. The English version of your statement in the third sentence it refers to 10.00 p.m., the time reference is 10.00 p.m., whereas the Albanian version refers to 8.00 p.m., 2000. Which time reference is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: 10.00 is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, taking those corrections --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that, I need to be guided to some of these to complete this. I don't have a statement with numbered paragraphs. Valbona is referred to where?

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: That's in -- in the English statement on page 2, and it's the third paragraph from the bottom, the very last word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: The name Fazli Rustemi appears on page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. I've lost my notes now. This is so confusing. One of these days you'll do this before the statement is finalised for the Court. The reference to Mahmuti, where is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: The reference to Mahmuti is on page 2, paragraph -- the third paragraph from the top. That's only in the Albanian version so it's correct in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The reference to Fazli.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Is on page 3, the fourth paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's correctly spelt. And the 10.00 p.m. reference is in the next paragraph, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's where the change is to the village name also; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: That's in the second statement. Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Mr. K81, taking those corrections into account, are the statements true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And can you confirm to this Court that that evidence is what you would give under oath today if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender Exhibit P2268 under seal. The exhibit contains the witness's statement dated May 30, 1999, and the corrections to the statement dated February 1st, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that a redacted version will be available almost instantly for publication.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we can make one available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think it's your duty to make one available simply by deleting the name. Meanwhile, it will be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I please have Exhibit P36 up on the screen. Can you zoom in a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Mr. K81, do you recognise the villages Zegra, Vladovo and Vlastica on this map? And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: -- with the help of the usher could you please make a line on the map to mark where you were hiding? Please show us the location of the mountains that you refer to in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: The mountains were around Llashtice and Zhegra villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Can you please mark the map. Oh, you did. Thank you. Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Could I have an IC number for this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC 111, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now please have Exhibit P1785 up on the screen. This exhibit is already in evidence. Please go to page 2 of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that to come up, Mr. K81, in your statement you described that you saw VJ soldiers who were looting and burning the village of Llashtice, and that you saw them burn the mosque in that village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Can you go to page 2 of that exhibit, please. The English one, if possible, because that's a colour copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Mr. K81, do you recognise the mosque on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes. This is the mosque in Llashtice village. It is this mosque that I saw being burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you have a copy of your statement there, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you look at the seventh paragraph. I take it the numbers are the same in Albanian and in English, Ms. Dragulev, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That paragraph in English reads: "In a nearby village named Zegra, I heard that a man's house was shot up." Who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard this from the villagers who were there nearby. This was an incident that occurred in that village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened during the days when the army came and took positions in Zhegra village. This is when his house was attacked and when this old man together with his wife were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you confirm when the -- the forces first arrived in Zhegra?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The forces arrived around 25th of March, but they kept coming. I think it was on the 29th when additional forces came to the village. I do not remember, though, the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you then in the next paragraph again talk about hearing what the army or civilians did, and in the paragraph after that you say that they also went to the home of the local president of the LDK. Who did you hear these things from? Was it the villagers you've mentioned, or was it from someone in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard it from the villagers. As large forces came there, we wanted to know what was going on. They started to attack the activists of the LDK, and we were scared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That answers the question. Thank you. And just one final question. If you go to the end of the statement and count back the sixth last paragraph says: "We left that village and went to the village of Zub. We wanted to get some food. Just as we sat down, the host of the house we were in said, The VJ was there, stand up." Is that what was said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what he said. The VJ was nearby. We wanted to look for food, and we were told that the army was nearby and that's why we had to leave and go somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when he said, "Stand up," what did he mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wanted to tell it us that the army was nearby and it was possible that they could catch us inside there and that that's why we had to leave.
