utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We will follow the indictment order again, Your Honour, for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the Milutinovic Defence has no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have just a few questions for this witness. May I ask the Registrar to place in e-court a Prosecution exhibit, namely 615, page 24. And can we zoom in on the right upper corner that refers to the town of Gnjilane, that shows Gnjilane and -- sorry. I think we have to show the next page, because that's where the border lies. Page 25, please. So now it's the left upper corner. Can we zoom in on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. K81, you saw a moment ago a different map but this one is a relief map, so it could be of more assistance. Do you recognise Zegra, Llashtice and Vladovo here? You mentioned them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you draw the area where you were, where the Crna Planina, Black Mountain, is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: This is the part where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we give this exhibit an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC 112, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In your statement, in paragraph 12 you said that the area where you were was three to four kilometres away from your village and that it is called Crna Planina. You said you had a pair of binoculars and that you could see what was happening in the environs from the position where you were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, in several paragraphs you describe the soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia, and you said that you could tell them apart since they wore dark green uniforms. Was it only because of that that you described them as VJ soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I could recognise the soldiers very well because I was there, and I could see them while they were in the village as well as while they were arriving in the village. And I also knew the uniforms they wore, so that's why I could recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Except for the uniforms you didn't see any insignia, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any insignia. I only saw their uniforms. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that you were able to see them while you were in your village, but it is your statement where we find that you were some three to four kilometres away from your village and some two to two and a half kilometres away from the other places, and that you could tell them apart by using your binoculars. That's what my question referred to. From that distance of over two kilometres, all you could see was their uniform, and based on that you concluded they were members of the VJ. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: As the crow flies, it was less than three or four kilometres. The road we used was longer. I would go as close as possible to see what was going on in the villages around that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was the shortest distance at which you were when you observed what was going on through the binoculars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Approximately 700, 800 metres. One kilometre at the most, not further than that. The mountains were there, and that was the closest I could get to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in your statement, you do not mention that you approached as close as that. In any case, tell me, please, whether you had the binoculars all the time and used it repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes, I had them with me all the time, and I used them because there was nothing else I could do. And I wanted to see what was happening for self-defence, fearing that they might enter our houses, and we were afraid they might come up to the place where we were hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: It is your testimony, therefore, that from the distance of 7 to 800 metres by using the binoculars you could clearly see what was going on to the extent described in your statement. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a few more questions for you. In paragraph 20, you say that you went to Presevo. Can you tell me whether you encountered any problems on the way, that is when you crossed from the territory of Kosovo over to Serbia proper, since you mention in your statement that Presevo is in Serbia proper and that it is an Albanian town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: We had problems only in Zub village where the army shot at us, but then we didn't see any more army until we arrived in Presheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I know. I asked you -- my question refers only to your trip as far as Presevo. Therefore, I believe you've answered it. I don't think I have any further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. K81, my name is Mihajlo Bakrac, attorney-at-law, counsel for General Lazarevic. I wanted to begin my cross-examination with what you stated at page 91, in line 3 and 4 of the transcript. When my colleague Mr. Aleksic asked you whether you had the binoculars all the time, you said yes. You said you wanted to use it for self-defence. Mr. K81, does that mean that you carried a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No, we didn't have weapons, but we observed what was happening in our village, what the army was doing, and the surrounding villages. None of us was armed, and that was why I kept the binoculars, only to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But you said that you used the binoculars for self-defence. What did you intend to defend with if you had no weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: A binocular is not a weapon. It can only helps you see what the army in this case was doing in my village, in Vlladovc, or in the surrounding villages. There is no way I could defend myself with a binocular, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm not saying you could use it for defence. I'm just quoting your words. You said you used the binoculars to organise your defence, which to me sounds like you were armed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No. No, I was not armed, but I just saw what was happening because they drove us out of our homes. That was why I was observing what was happening, fearing that they might come up to the mountain where we were hiding. So that was the only reason I kept the binoculars and used them all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say you kept the binoculars, what are you trying to tell us? Whose binoculars? How did you come to possess it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: The binocular was mine, and I had them since a long time ago. They didn't belong to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. K81, you stated that you did not serve your military term. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Because at that time I was still very young, and I was not invited to join it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. K81, at the time of the war you were 24 or 25. People are being called to serve as early as 18.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: But I was never summoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you receive a draft call from the KLA headquarters, perhaps, to join them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did they ask any vehicles from you or some other type of assistance for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No, they didn't ask me for any vehicles, for anything for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But you knew the KLA people from your area, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: In my area I didn't know anyone, and as far as I know, there were no KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know Imeri Alisa from your village of Vladovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How about Alija Ahmet from -- from Gnjilane?

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness indicated that the translation was not working. It seems to be working now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know Alija Ahmet from Gornja Livoca [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you give that answer again, please. The interpreter didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know Ahmet Aliu from Livoc e Eperm [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since you said I knew Imeri Alisa, did you know that he was a member of the KLA and his pseudonym was Ili?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No, I never knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was he hiding in the mountains with you, the mountains you mentioned in your statement? Was he one of the group hiding in the mountains?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No, he was not one of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. How many were there, and were all of you male?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: In the mountain, there were women, children, elderly people, young people, males. All the people who were in the village, they all took to the mountains, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Except for your family, and your family went to the village of Vlastica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: My family, Llashtice village were in that area, in a mountainous area. There were no KLA members. There were only ordinary villagers unarmed who were driven out of the place by the Yugoslav forces. They were driven out of their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. K81, you stated that the Yugoslav forces were quartered in the battery factory. Where is that factory? Is it in your village or some other village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No. The battery village is at the entrance to the Zhegra village. One kilometre or so from Vlladovc village. That was where they were stationed. And after that, they started to maltreat people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say they were stationed there, what do you mean? Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you personally go to the factory? Did you see the forces quartered there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: When the army started to come, the Serbian army, I was in Zhegra. I saw them taking opposition. But when they were stationed and started maltreating people, we didn't dare go up to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. K81, in your statement, at page 5 you stated, and I will not mention her name, in any case, you state there that your sister provided a statement to the OTP investigators. Is that correct as well? I do not receive interpretation. I'm not receiving it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If need be, we can put this up on e-court, but did you know that your sister stated to the OTP investigators that between Vladovo and Zegra there is a battery factory owned by the state? On that Friday, paramilitary members took over the factory and used it as their base. Did you know that she stated that, claiming that paramilitary forces were at the factory? And the statement was given under the pseudonym K8, for my learned friends from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what my sister had stated, but the fact is that that was a battery factory and that is where the Serbian army was operating. But there were also Serbian villagers who accompanied them, and they were under the command of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How do you know they were under the command of the Serbian army? First of all, you didn't see them there. This is what you said a moment ago. So where did you get that information that they were under the command of the Serbian army? You haven't stated any such thing up until now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I saw the army with my eyes, but everything was done under the army's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The fact that you saw the army there with your own eyes is a different story. How do you know that everything was done under army orders? Did you see any order of that nature? Where do you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I saw it with my own eyes. When I was going to Zhegra, before I went back I saw the army with the Serbian civilians, and I saw that they were cooperating with one another. And when the army attacked the Vlladovc village, it was the army who did everything. That was in the front line. In Llashtice, too, I saw them when they entered the village. There were soldiers and civilians, but they were under the control of the army, under the command of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You saw them enter the village, but you didn't see them do anything else. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I saw them setting the houses on fire, the mosque. I saw them looting and raiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you were in the village of Vlastica and you saw it all, or did you see it from the mountain, from the distance of some three to four kilometres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I stayed in the mountain near Llashtice, but Zhegra village and Llashtice village are situated around that place where I was hiding. So when I wanted to see what was going on in Zhegra village, I went to that side of the mountain overlooking Zhegra and so on. I moved from one place to another and observed the developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your statement at page 2, did you not say the following, and this was in May 1999 when your recollection was far better: "The VJ soldiers behaved like proper soldiers. They minded their own business and behaved properly." Isn't that a part of your statement? Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is what I have stated, and this is how it was. But until they were stationed, after that they immediately started the maltreatment, and I have explained everything in my statement. After that, the incidents started, the maltreatment of the population that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Everything you could see you could see from up there in the mountains; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Most of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And from that location as you confirmed to my learned friend, you couldn't notice or make out any insignia or patches worn by the soldiers in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: What insignia or patches do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Uniform, the uniform patches.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see them. I saw only the army. I could see the army and the police, but I couldn't discern the insignia. Had I paid greater attention maybe I would have seen, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the members of the paramilitary forces also wore uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I couldn't distinguish the paramilitary forces, but I saw people partly dressed in uniform operating in -- in unison with the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I will read out a part of your sister's statement: "Some wore olive-drab military uniforms and some had olive-drab T-shirts. 10 soldiers had painted their faces. Most of them had insignia I'd never seen before. They were the shape of a lion, although I cannot say that with certainty. It was no regular insignia of the VJ. Everyone around me kept saying that these were Arkan's Tigers." Did you know that your sister provided that description?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: I told you earlier, and I am repeating it, I do not know what my sister said. At that time, she was here and she gave her own statement. She spoke about what she saw from Llashtice. She passed to Pashen [phoen], Gudrik [phoen], Partesh [phoen], Gllogovc, and she could see what was happening in these Serb-inhabited villages. So I don't know what she said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But she was not up at the mountain. She didn't have the binoculars. She was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is no way to cross-examine this witness with reference to another person's statement. You can lead that evidence in due course if you wish. You've asked him enough questions about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to ask the witness this:

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Qamil Shabani.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you spoke of the events that the -- that His Honour asked you about when you heard that in the village of Zegra soldiers came to a house of an LDK activist and that he was not at home at that moment and that his name was Nehat, did you hear all that from Qamil Shabani or from someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: No. I heard it from someone else when the Serbian army went to search for him as an activist of the democratic league of a party that was in Kosova. Nehat was not at home, so they killed his father, the uncle, and the uncle's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you stated here that you heard the soldiers had done that. Mr. Shabani provided his own statement to this Tribunal, and as regards the same event, he said that paramilitary members in Zegra --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, this is not the way to cross-examine a witness on what he has said in his statement. If you have a point to put to him, put it, but this lengthy reading of the statement of another person is not the appropriate way to do this. If there's a particular point you want to make, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have that witness's statement, and I can also check against the transcript. I have passed 7.00. I will not have any further questions, but I can only provide you with some explanation as to this witness's statement at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can lead that witness in due course or produce the statement if we agree to accept it when it comes to the Defence case, but if you have a particular point to put to this witness that is the case and get his comment on it, please put it, but don't read out the statement of another witness. We trust you to have a basis for your question. Just get to the point of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I've received his answers as regards his sister's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What if I told you that there is a witness from Zegra who says that he or she was in Zegra at the time and that the paramilitaries were responsible for the incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: My answer is this, and I told you earlier what the other witnesses have told you I don't know. I'm here to tell you what I personally know. In Zhegra and in the surrounding villages there was the Yugoslav army operating. All of them were in uniforms, but they were aided also by the Serb villagers of these villages. I don't know what the other person has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the height of his evidence in any event is that he heard from villagers that either the army or civilians went to the home of the -- of Nehat. Now, he's not saying it was the army, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation we received, or the translation, was the army and civilians. Let me check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. You are right. Not "and civilians," but "or civilians." I apologise to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there isn't a point to be pursued here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Ms. Dragulev?

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Just one quick question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 of your statement on page 1, you stated that the men in civilian clothes that you were told were Arkan's Tigers stayed with the VJ soldiers, did you see that for yourself? Did you see that or did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: When the vehicles of the Serbian army came, I heard from some villagers who were older than me, they told me that these were Arkan's Tigers or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: And did you see these people stay with VJ soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DRAGULEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: K81, that brings your evidence to a conclusion. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to give it and to add to the statement you already gave. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic -- sorry, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We're running late, but I just wanted to draw your attention to the following: After expert Brunborg, we have Zlatomir Pesic. We have just received a statement of the 29th of June, 2005, on four pages he gave to the interim administration of the UN in Kosovo, and supplemental information on two pages with 20 paragraphs. If he is to begin testifying tomorrow, according to the schedule, I believe this will pose problems for us. I need to discuss this with Mr. Ackerman. Nonetheless, I believe he would support my statement, my application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You perhaps ought to speak directly to the Prosecution about it to see if in fact there is a way of accommodating any difficulty you may have by rearranging other witnesses' evidence. We note that this fits in neatly at the moment with Prosecution plans to call Brunborg as the first witness on Wednesday, tomorrow at 2.15. So we now adjourn until 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.09 p.m.,
